name: Niacin (nicotinic acid)
short: Dose-dependent flushing, gastrointestinal upset and liver dysfunction are reported; in a meta-analysis of 11 trials niacin therapy was associated with more new-onset diabetes (risk ratio 1.34).
text: An overview of 14 reviews found that oral niacin and nicotinamide were associated with a range of adverse effects, including gastrointestinal upset, liver dysfunction, flushing, skin rash and fatigue; these were more common at higher doses, more frequent with niacin than with nicotinamide, and mostly diminished or resolved when the dose was reduced or stopped, although the authors noted that side effects have rarely been examined systematically. A meta-analysis of 47 articles (11 741 individuals) reported that in healthy individuals taking nicotinic acid alone, major adverse effects occurred at doses below 1000 mg a day, whereas in people with dyslipidaemia or cardiovascular disease adverse events with nicotinic acid alone occurred at doses above those used with other treatments; the authors concluded that the results may indicate a high degree of conservativeness in existing upper intake levels for nicotinic acid, and the abstract notes that higher doses are associated with adverse effects, especially flushing. In a meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials with 26 340 participants without diabetes, niacin therapy given for cardiovascular indications was associated with a moderately increased risk of new-onset diabetes (risk ratio 1.34), equivalent to one additional case per 43 people treated for 5 years, regardless of background statin therapy. The overview noted that tolerability is limited in people with conditions such as renal dysfunction. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
